html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation; HTML: hypertext markup language

  • The stages of a RAG pipeline and what can go wrong at each
  • Chunking strategies and sizes
  • Indexing: embeddings, keyword (BM25) and hybrid indexes, metadata
  • Contextual retrieval and freshness management
  • When not to use RAG

2The Pipeline

Running case

Lumen Advisory Builds a Knowledge Assistant for a Law-Adjacent Compliance Team

  • 30,000 pages of regulations, internal policies and past rulings, updated weekly
  • Analysts need cited answers with exact clause numbers
  • After one weekly refresh the assistant starts giving confident wrong answers

Stage Purpose Typical failure
Ingest and parse Read PDFs, HTML, tables Lost tables, scanned pages, broken order
Clean Remove boilerplate, deduplicate Repeated headers dominate results
Chunk Split into retrievable units Chunks too big (diluted) or too small (no context)
Enrich Add metadata and context Missing source, date, section
Embed and index Vectors plus keyword index Mismatched embeddings; stale index
Retrieve Find candidates Misses exact identifiers; irrelevant hits
Rerank Reorder by relevance Skipped; latency added
Generate with citations Answer from the chunks Unsupported claims; wrong citations
  • Offline half (ingest to index) and online half (retrieve to answer) fail differently; separate their monitoring.
  • Diagnose from the symptom: confident wrong answers after a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point first to retrieval or indexing (stale, missing or mismatched chunks), not to the model.
Exam tip

When quality drops after a data refresh and the model is unchanged, investigate the retrieval and indexing step first.

3Chunking

Strategy How Best for Risk
Fixed size with overlap Equal token windows, small overlap Uniform text; baseline Cuts clauses and tables in half
Structure-aware Split on headings, sections, clauses, rows Regulations, manuals, code Uneven sizes
Semantic Split where topics change Narrative text Extra processing
Hierarchical (parent-child) Retrieve small chunks, return the larger parent Precision plus context More storage and logic
Special handling Tables, code, lists kept intact Structured content Parser effort
  • Chunks are usually no more than a few hundred tokens; size, boundaries and overlap all change retrieval quality. Test sizes on your data.
  • Too large: relevance is diluted and context is wasted. Too small: meaning is lost ("the fee is 2%" without whose fee).
  • Keep units whole: a clause, a table with its header, a function.
  • Store metadata: source, section path, date, version, access group, language. Metadata enables filtering and citations.

4Indexing

Choice Guidance
Embeddings Anthropic offers no embedding model; use a provider such as Voyage AI (general, multilingual, code, finance, law, multimodal, contextualized chunk models) and evaluate vendors on your data [Verify live]
Query vs document Embed with the right input_type (query or document) for retrieval
Similarity Normalized vectors: cosine = dot product
Dimension and quantization Smaller dimensions or int8/binary quantization cut storage (4x to 32x) with some accuracy cost
Vector index Fast approximate nearest-neighbor search over embeddings
Keyword index (BM25) Lexical ranking; strong for exact identifiers, codes, names
Hybrid Combine vector and BM25 scores; best general default
Domain models Legal, finance, code embeddings help specialized corpora

Contextual retrieval

  • A chunk like "the fee rose 3%" loses meaning out of context. Contextual retrieval has Claude write 50 to 100 tokens of document-level context for each chunk and prepend it before embedding and before the BM25 index.
  • Reported results (failure rate = 1 minus recall@20, baseline 5.7%): contextual embeddings -35%; with contextual BM25 -49%; with reranking -67%.
  • Prompt caching makes this cheap: load the document once and reference it for every chunk.
  • Rerank: retrieve a larger candidate set (for example 150), rerank, pass the top K (for example 20) to the model; more chunks help up to a point, then distract. Reranking adds some latency.

5Freshness, Security and Evaluation

Concern Practice
Freshness Incremental re-indexing; version documents; delete removed content; re-embed when the embedding model changes (never mix spaces); validate after each refresh
Access control Store access metadata; filter retrieval by the user's permissions (Module 8)
Prompt injection Retrieved text is untrusted data: tag it, state that, limit tool power
Citations Return source and location; verify that quoted text exists
Evaluation Measure retrieval (recall@k, precision) separately from generation (faithfulness, correctness)
Monitoring Index age, empty-result rate, rerank scores, citation validity

When not to use RAG

  • If the knowledge base is under about 200,000 tokens (roughly 500 pages), consider putting it in the prompt with caching instead.
  • Use RAG when the corpus is larger, changes often, or needs per-user access filtering and citations to sources.
Exam tip

Quality drops after a data or embedding change with the model unchanged: check retrieval and indexing first.

Exam tip

Under about 200,000 tokens, a cached prompt may beat building RAG.

6Exam Q&A

S1After a team switches to a new embedding provider, a support assistant starts citing passages about the wrong products. Prompts, model and latency are unchanged, and the ingestion jobs report success. What should the architect check first?

  • AWhether the stored document vectors were re-embedded with the new provider so queries and documents share one vector space
  • BWhether the generation model has quietly been replaced by a weaker snapshot
  • CWhether the context window of the model has been reduced
  • DWhether the temperature value was changed during the migration
Show the answer

Answer: A. Vectors from different embedding models are incompatible, so retrieval returns poor matches while everything else looks healthy.

S2Exact statute numbers and clause identifiers are being missed by an embeddings-only retriever. What is the best improvement?

  • AIncrease the embedding dimension of the existing index so that exact identifiers become more distinctive
  • BSwitch to a larger generation model
  • CLower the chunk overlap to zero so that every chunk is shorter and identifiers appear only once
  • DAdd a BM25 keyword index and combine it with the vector index (hybrid search)
Show the answer

Answer: D. Lexical search catches exact identifiers that embeddings can miss.

S3Chunks such as "the fee increased by 3 percent" retrieve poorly because the surrounding context is lost. Which technique addresses this directly?

  • ARemove metadata from the chunks
  • BTruncate all chunks to one sentence
  • CContextual retrieval: prepend chunk-specific context before embedding and BM25 indexing
  • DIncrease top-K from 20 to 200 without reranking, so that the relevant chunk is certain to be included
Show the answer

Answer: C. A short, document-level context line prepended before embedding and keyword indexing restores the meaning that the chunk lost.

S4A corpus of 60,000 tokens changes monthly and has no per-user access rules. What is a reasonable design?

  • APlace it in the prompt as a cached prefix, without building a RAG pipeline
  • BBuild a full vector pipeline with reranking and a cluster, then re-index it every time a document changes
  • CFine-tune a model on it every month
  • DSplit it into 1,000 tiny chunks and retrieve randomly
Show the answer

Answer: A. Below about 200,000 tokens, a cached prompt can be simpler and faster.

S5Which TWO are required when the embedding model is replaced? Select TWO.

  • AKeep the old document vectors and embed only new queries with the new model
  • BRe-embed the corpus with the new model so that queries and documents share one vector space
  • CRe-evaluate retrieval quality on a test set before cutting over
  • DRemove the keyword index
  • EMix old and new vectors in one index to save time
Show the answer

Answer: B, C. Vectors from different models are incompatible; validate before switching.

S6A table in a PDF is split between two chunks and answers about it are wrong. What is the best fix?

  • AUse structure-aware chunking that keeps the table with its header intact
  • BIncrease the overlap on all chunks
  • CConvert the table to an image and skip chunking altogether, relying on the model to read the picture
  • DUse a larger model to guess the missing rows
Show the answer

Answer: A. Structure-aware chunking keeps a table together with its header, so retrieval returns the whole table instead of a fragment.

S7Which design lets the system return precise passages while still giving the model enough context?

  • AUsing only very large chunks everywhere so that every answer can include a lot of surrounding text
  • BUsing only single-sentence chunks everywhere
  • CHierarchical chunking: retrieve small child chunks and return their larger parent
  • DReturning random neighbors of the best chunk
Show the answer

Answer: C. Retrieving small child chunks and returning their larger parent balances precision with the context the model needs.

S8A user-specific restriction must hold in a RAG system. Where should it be enforced?

  • AIn retrieval, by filtering on access metadata for the authenticated user
  • BIn the system prompt, by asking the model to ignore restricted passages that it should not show anyone
  • CIn the response, by asking the model to redact restricted text
  • DIn the embedding model, by training it on allowed documents only
Show the answer

Answer: A. Enforce access in code before the model sees data.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Pipeline Ingest · clean · chunk · enrich · embed and index · retrieve · rerank · generate with citations
Diagnose Wrong answers after a refresh: check retrieval and index first
Chunks A few hundred tokens; keep units whole; metadata for filtering and citation
Strategies Fixed with overlap · structure-aware · semantic · hierarchical
Index Vector plus BM25 (hybrid); embed with the right input_type; no Anthropic embedding model
Contextual retrieval 50 to 100 tokens of context; failure -35%, -49%, -67% with BM25 and rerank
Rerank Retrieve about 150, pass top 20
No RAG Under about 200,000 tokens: cached prompt
Freshness Incremental re-index; re-embed on model change; filter by access
